item.title: Resolving and Suppressing Temporally Correlated Noise in Quantum Error Correction
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates the first scalable mitigation of temporally correlated errors on a 105‑qubit superconducting processor, showing that surface‑code logical memory can retain its time‑domain error suppression as the code size grows from 3×3 to 7×7 patches. By identifying and modeling leakage into the third excited state and introducing a “walking” stability circuit, the authors push the logical error floor down to ≤3.2 × 10⁻⁸ over 60 cycles—two orders of magnitude better than conventional approaches—and reveal that remaining failures are dominated by rare ionizing‑radiation bursts. The adaptive termination scheme further trims spacetime overhead, highlighting a practical pathway toward fault‑tolerant quantum computers that must control both spatial and temporal error channels.

Scaling fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC) requires suppressing errors in both space and time, yet standard logical memory experiments primarily probe spatial faults. Here, we use a 105-qubit Willow superconducting quantum processor to realize and scale the surface code stability experiment, which is alternatively sensitive to temporal error chains. Scaling from patch sizes of $3 \times 3$ to $7 \times 7$, we realize a timelike block suppression factor of $μ_T = 1.47 \pm 0.25$, demonstrating the ability to maintain temporal error suppression as the number of qubits increases. By extending the stability experiment for many cycles, we uncover a sum-of-exponentials behavior in error suppression caused by a temporally correlated error: data-qubit heating to the third excited state $|3\rangle$. We fully capture this effect with a parameter-free, device-level leakage model incorporating higher-state transport during syndrome extraction cycles. To suppress this error, we develop and realize a walking stability circuit, reaching a logical error probability floor of $\le 3.20\times 10^{-8}$ at 60 cycles---two orders of magnitude below the standard construction---and limited by ionizing radiation error bursts. Finally, by adaptively terminating syndrome extraction based on decoder confidence in an offline analysis, we reduce spacetime logical error by 38% and time overhead by 34% compared to the optimal fixed-cycle strategy.

item.title: Optimal Quantum Sensing Algorithms for Discrete-Frequency Spectroscopy
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that by tailoring quantum‑sensing protocols to the structure of a discrete‑frequency spectroscopy problem, one can achieve a provable √N advantage over traditional frequency‑by‑frequency scans—a speedup that rivals the best known quantum‑algorithmic gains for search problems. The work bridges recent hardware progress in nitrogen‑vacancy and other single‑qubit sensors with algorithmic design, demonstrating that even a lone qubit under simple π‑pulse control can reach optimal detection performance while full learning of spectra demands coherent processing on a small quantum processor. If the predicted two‑order‑of‑magnitude reductions in measurement time hold experimentally, molecular‐screening and other high‑throughput spectroscopic applications could become dramatically more efficient, though real‑world noise and calibration errors will still set practical limits.

Spectroscopy is a versatile tool that drives scientific discovery and underpins modern technologies. Quantum sensing offers promising opportunities to advance spectroscopy through enhanced sensitivity and spectral and spatial resolution. However, existing approaches largely focus on improving general measurement capabilities, often overlooking the structure of specific sensing tasks and leaving potential performance gains untapped. Here, we develop an algorithmic approach to quantum sensing tailored to various spectroscopic tasks, providing new avenues for improvement. Specifically, we consider general time-varying signals supported on a known set of $N$ candidate frequencies, a setting we call discrete-frequency spectroscopy. We formulate three types of practically motivated sensing tasks---Detection, Search, and Learning---that require progressively more spectral information. For all tasks, we design optimal quantum sensing algorithms achieving a $\sqrt{N}$ speedup over conventional frequency-scanning approaches. Optimal Detection and Search need only a single-qubit sensor under $π$-pulse control, whereas optimal Learning provably requires coherent processing with a quantum computer. End-to-end numerical simulations incorporating various experimental imperfections predict up to two-orders-of-magnitude speedup in Detection. As an example, we analyze the feasibility of our Detection and Search algorithms for real-world molecular screening based on state-of-the-art nitrogen-vacancy centers. We also show how quantum-computing-enhanced Learning enables wireless communication in a weak-signal regime where conventional methods fail. Our results establish a practical route toward realizing quantum advantages via designing task-specific sensing algorithms.

item.title: Benchmarking memory and nonlinear processing capacity of quantum recurrent neural networks for time series prediction
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article provides one of the first systematic benchmarks of variational quantum recurrent neural networks, showing that they can match classical RNNs on standard memory‑and‑nonlinearity tasks while still lagging in scaling efficiency. By introducing a task‑driven capacity metric, the authors connect QRNN performance to recent advances in quantum reservoir computing and highlight how careful parameter initialization can unlock higher processing power—a nuance that mirrors broader challenges in training deep variational circuits. The work signals both promise and practical hurdles for quantum time‑series models, giving researchers a concrete framework to gauge where future architectural innovations might finally deliver an advantage over classical sequence learners.

Quantum machine learning has emerged as a promising approach to time series prediction. While quantum reservoir computing has been widely explored for this setting, variational quantum models tailored to sequential data remain comparatively understudied, largely because they are difficult to train. In this work, we present a rigorous benchmark of variational quantum recurrent neural networks (QRNNs) on time series prediction tasks, focusing on two key capabilities: memory and nonlinear processing. We introduce a task-driven methodology that quantifies model capacity, enabling an intuitive and fair comparison across architectures, including classical recurrent baselines. We evaluate the proposed framework on two generic benchmark tasks and on a synthetic dataset describing a chaotic system. Overall, the quantum models achieve performance comparable to their classical counterparts, but classical models scale better with the memory size within the range studied. Notably, one QRNN variant shows higher average capacity on the task designed to jointly probe memory and nonlinear capacity. Moreover, our results show that quantum models offer better capacity when we are able to find a good parameter initialization. However, the increasing sensitivity to initialization leads to a lower probability of finding good solutions as the model size increases. These results provide a principled starting point for designing richer quantum recurrent architectures and for assessing where they may offer practical benefits.

item.title: The speed limit of gravitational entanglement and the cost of noise
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pinpoints the fundamental rate at which two massive objects can become entangled solely through their mutual gravity, showing that—even in an ideal noiseless world—the speed drops as the inverse cube of their separation and that realistic environmental noise pushes the scaling down to an even steeper inverse‑fourth law. By deriving exact limits for continuous error‑correction schemes, it clarifies how much decoherence must be suppressed before a tabletop test can decisively rule out classical‑gravity explanations, linking the proposal directly to ongoing efforts by groups such as those at UChicago and Vienna. The results give experimentalists concrete benchmarks for mass size, distance, and coherence time, while also tempering expectations with the stark trade‑off that protecting against noise simultaneously hides the very gravitational signal they seek.

Is gravity quantum? A proposed test lets two small masses, each in a superposition of two places, become entangled through their mutual gravity. Gravity is weak, so the masses must stay coherent for seconds while random forces disturb them. Here we ask how fast gravity can entangle two masses, and what noise costs. Without noise we find the maximum rate exactly: it falls as the inverse cube of the separation, and two positions per mass achieve it. Above a noise level set by the masses and their separation, gravity's leading pull can be imitated by classical signals, and every strategy is limited to a rate falling at least as the inverse fourth power. Exact, continuous error correction shields the masses from noise but hides them from each other: the best rate falls as the inverse seventh power, and six positions on a hexagon come within 10% of it at large separation.

item.title: Entanglement distillation, nonlocal magic, and state sharing in an isospectral non-Hermitian bipartite model
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers the first exact, many‑copy formulas for entanglement‑distillable rates and CHSH violations in a deliberately engineered non‑Hermitian two‑qubit model that mimics realistic dephasing and circuit noise. By showing that correlated PPT catalysts cannot boost Bell‑pair yields and providing closed‑form magic‑state concentration probabilities, it bridges abstract resource‑theory results with the practical limits faced by near‑term superconducting or trapped‑ion hardware. The work therefore offers a rare benchmark for testing error‑mitigation strategies and for calibrating how much nonlocal “magic” can be harvested from noisy qubits before fault‑tolerant thresholds are reached.

An invertible nonunitary similarity deformation leaves a two-qubit Hamiltonian's spectrum unchanged while varying a selected normalized right eigenstate in the fixed physical inner product. We embed this state in a two-parameter maximally correlated family that includes local dephasing and noisy circuit preparation. Hashing and a matching diagonal relative-entropy bound give the exact distillable entanglement and the PPT comparison distances at every finite tensor power. Correlated PPT catalysts cannot improve the Bell-pair distillation rate. The optimized CHSH value is \(2\sqrt{1+t^2}\): every state with nonzero coherence violates CHSH, while complete dephasing is separable. A calibrated finite-sample bound and two equal-fidelity preparations clarify which noise parameters determine the rate. For pure inputs, the binomial Schmidt spectrum gives logarithmic collectively optimized nonlocal magic with vanishing density, despite a positive entanglement density and extensive pairwise-frame magic. Fixed Clifford decoding gives six- and eight-copy CCZ concentration probabilities \(P_6=\frac12(1-2^{-\mathcal M_γ})\) and \(P_8=1-2^{-\mathcal M_γ}\). The same family permits explicit swapping recursions, symmetry-resolved entanglement, and a comparison of qubit stabilizer and fermionic Gaussian resources. These calculations keep the relevant operation classes separate when comparing many-copy limits.

item.title: Experimental simulation of a Hilbert-space inner-product change
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks the first experimental demonstration of a controllable change in a qubit’s Hilbert‑space inner product, moving beyond earlier PT‑symmetric simulations that kept the metric fixed and opening a new route for probing non‑Hermitian physics on quantum hardware. By implementing the IP‑change channel with both a qutrit encoding and a two‑qubit Stinespring dilation, and by establishing a rigorous fidelity threshold that excludes trivial mixtures of unitaries, the work shows how subtle metric transformations can be verified even in noisy superconducting processors. The clear benefit of readout error mitigation—raising successful instances from 14 to 24 out of 40—highlights an immediate practical lesson for any near‑term experiment that seeks to explore exotic quantum dynamics beyond standard unitary evolution.

We simulate an effective change in a single qubit's inner product (IP) by implementing the channel $\mathcal{F}^η$ on a superconducting quantum processor. Whereas previous experiments simulated parity-time (PT)-symmetric dynamics with a fixed IP, this experiment implements the IP-change channel itself for metrics associated with PT-symmetric systems. Building on an earlier adversarial verification approach, we derive a process-fidelity threshold that rules out mixtures of qubit unitary operations with random discarding of runs. We test the channel for 40 metrics using a single qutrit and a two-qubit Stinespring dilation. The measured fidelities exceed the threshold in 24 of 40 qutrit instances after readout error mitigation, compared with 16 of 40 unmitigated two-qubit instances. Without mitigation, 14 of 40 qutrit instances pass. These results demonstrate a direct simulation of an effective Hilbert-space IP change and its verification against a specified adversarial class, while showing the importance of readout treatment in comparing the encodings.

item.title: Rethinking Entropic Uncertainty: How measuring without a trace leads to longer keys
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that by treating Alice and Bob as a single system and adding a virtual measurement register, the entropic uncertainty relation can be extended to incorporate any number of mutually unbiased bases, delivering provably tighter QKD key rates against coherent attacks. The technique not only resolves a long‑standing gap in multi‑basis security analysis but also offers a versatile tool for strengthening proofs across many quantum cryptographic and sensing protocols. As a result, future implementations that already employ multiple measurement settings can now extract longer secret keys without hardware changes, though the approach still relies on idealized virtual measurements that must be carefully mapped onto real‑world devices.

In recent years, the entropic uncertainty relation (EUR) has been one of the most prominent tools to obtain tight key rates secure against general coherent attacks for a broad class of quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols. Despite its success, the fundamental question of how to incorporate the statistics of more than two mutually unbiased bases (MUBs) directly into the EUR is yet to be answered. Here, we introduce a simple yet powerful shift of perspective: Instead of the usual tripartition into the systems of Alice, Bob and Eve, we treat Alice and Bob as one joint system and introduce an additional register as the third system. This register contains the results of appropriately chosen virtual measurements that leave no trace in the real branch of the protocol, but act as a conditioning on the counterfactual phase error measurements. We show that this allows us to obtain tight key rates for QKD protocols using an arbitrary number of MUBs directly and natively from the EUR. Moreover, we demonstrate that this approach has a much broader relevance beyond the inclusion of multiple MUBs, allowing for improvements in many existing security proofs and the treatment of previously unexplored aspects for a wide range of protocols.

item.title: Quantitative measurement of microwave power at millikelvin temperatures: Comparison between dispersively and directly coupled superconducting qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that superconducting transmon qubits can serve as calibrated microwave‑power sensors at millikelvin temperatures, directly comparing the performance of qubits coupled straight to a feedline versus those read out dispersively. By spanning a dynamic range from –155 dBm up to –55 dBm, the dual‑coupling device provides a practical way to measure line attenuation and drive strength—key parameters for achieving high‑fidelity gates as quantum processors scale. The approach builds on recent work integrating quantum sensors into hardware stacks, offering a simpler cryogenic metrology tool while highlighting that dispersive readout carries larger uncertainty than direct coupling. Readers should care because accurate power calibration underpins error budgeting and reproducibility across quantum computing experiments.

The Rabi frequency of a two-level system is directly proportional to the electric field amplitude being incident on this system. Taking advantage of this relationship, it is possible to use two-level systems as quantitative sensors of electric fields. Here, we apply this concept to superconducting qubits and use them for quantitative measurement of microwave power at millikelvin temperatures. Our superconducting circuit design includes three transmon qubits directly coupled to the central microwave feedline and three transmon qubits coupled dispersively via readout resonators to the feedline. We compare both coupling schemes to assess their reliability for microwave power sensing. Further, we describe the modeling behind each power-sensing method, including an uncertainty estimation based upon repeated measurements. By combining dispersively coupled and directly coupled qubits on the same device, we are able to explore different power ranges: from $-155\;$dBm to $-130\;$dBm for the directly coupled qubits and from $-95\;$dBm to $-55\;$dBm for the dispersively coupled qubits. When determining the microwave-line attenuation for a frequency of $6.0\;$GHz from room temperature to the millikelvin stage of the cryostat, we obtain best estimates and uncertainties for the directly coupled transmons of $(74.7\pm 0.2) \;$dB and for the dispersively coupled transmons of $(75.4\pm 6.8) \;$dB. The larger uncertainty of the dispersively coupled qubit measurements indicates that these qubits are less reliable for power sensing than the directly coupled qubits, most likely, due to the additional coupling resonator, whose transfer function is difficult to estimate accurately. Our results constitute the first step towards validation of qubit power sensing in dilution fridges, leading towards traceability for cryogenic microwave measurements.

item.title: Sequential strategy for depolarizing strength estimation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that repeatedly feeding the same probe through a depolarizing channel can linearly boost the quantum Fisher information for very low noise and even let a single‑qubit probe outperform optimal two‑qubit schemes once three or more repetitions are used, highlighting a surprisingly simple route to sharper noise‑parameter estimates. By identifying an optimal finite number of channel applications in the weak‑noise regime, the work connects directly to current efforts to calibrate and mitigate errors on NISQ hardware where precise depolarizing‑strength knowledge is essential for error‑correction thresholds and quantum sensing protocols. The results suggest that sequential encoding—already easy to implement on existing platforms—could become a practical tool for faster, more accurate characterization of noisy channels without the overhead of entangled multi‑qubit probes.

We study the advantages of applying a sequential strategy for enhancing the precision in estimating the strength $p$ of a depolarizing channel, using qudit and two-qubit probes. The sequential strategy requires that the same depolarizing channel is repeatedly applied $M$ times to the quantum probe. From the analysis of the probe's output state, both the quantum Fisher information (QFI) and its regularization RQFI, given from multiplication by $p$, are analyzed. We determine that in the limit of $p \to 0$, the QFI is {\it linearly amplified} with the number of channel repetitions. Instead, in the weak-noise regime, the QFI is maximized at a finite value of $M$. Then, the RQFI decreases more quickly with $p$ as $M$ increases. In particular, for two-qubit probes, the RQFI decreases with the depolarization strength proportionally to the amount of correlation between the qubits. item.title: SCOPE: A Physical Execution Latency-Guided Quantum Circuit Compilation Framework
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces SCOPE, a compiler that uses an operator‑Schmidt time surrogate to steer pulse‑level optimization toward the shortest possible execution latency, directly addressing the coherence‑time bottleneck that limits near‑term quantum processors. By integrating a physics‑based lower bound on nonlocal evolution into a genetic search, SCOPE achieves up to a two‑fold reduction in critical‑path duration compared with the previous EPOC framework across a range of benchmark circuits, including a six‑qubit QFT. The results demonstrate that latency‑aware compilation can translate into tangible speedups without increasing gate count, highlighting a practical pathway for squeezing more algorithmic depth out of noisy hardware. However, the approach depends on accurate coupling models and incurs extra classical optimization overhead, so its benefits will be most pronounced when pulse‑level control is already available on the target device.

Quantum computing requires compilers to translate algorithms represented in the quantum circuit model into unitary operations supported by physical devices. Limited coherence time makes physical execution latency an important compilation objective. Gate fusion can shorten pulses, but gate count and depth do not capture fused targets' control demands. Evaluating every candidate with quantum optimal control (QOC) would embed pulse optimization in structural search. We present Schmidt-guided Compilation for Optimized Pulse Execution (SCOPE), driven by an operator Schmidt time surrogate. The target's angular distance from product operators measures the required nonlocal change; dividing it by a coupling-limited evolution-rate bound gives a lower bound on exact implementation time. Trace-angle and waveform constraints complete block scores for critical-path evaluation during genetic search. Local QOC determines final pulse durations. Under a numerical nearest-neighbor control model, all 104 results across 13 instances from four application families have shorter QOC critical-path durations than an adapted efficient pulse generation framework with advanced synthesis for quantum circuits (EPOC). Using eight-run instance means, the equally weighted reduction is 42.50\%, with a geometric mean speedup of 2.00. In a shared six-qubit quantum Fourier transform (QFT) ablation, time-surrogate guidance reduces mean QOC duration by 22.21\% relative to gate-count guidance and 21.01\% relative to depth guidance, validating the surrogate's joint use in fitness evaluation and mutation-region selection.

item.title: What kind of quantum advantage is this?
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a growing source of confusion in the field by offering a clear taxonomy that separates the underlying mechanisms—structural, interference‑based, and coherent—from how essential they are for achieving a genuine quantum advantage. By formalising a diagnostic framework and an entanglement‑breaking test, it gives researchers a practical tool to evaluate new algorithmic claims against the strongest classical adversaries, something that has been missing amid recent “quantum supremacy” debates. The approach also clarifies why certain problems like the hidden subgroup case demand cross‑copy coherence, helping the community focus effort on truly novel quantum resources rather than superficial speedups.

Quantum advantage encompasses fundamentally different claims, from resource reductions to exponential separations in sample complexity. Evaluating these claims requires distinguishing how an algorithm achieves an advantage from what is necessary for the separation and how strongly it is supported against classical alternatives. We propose a multi-label taxonomy that makes these distinctions explicit, classifying structural, interference, and coherent mechanisms while separately recording their necessity and the evidence for the classical comparison. Coherent mechanisms are further divided into memory and output, reflecting distinct restrictions on quantum information processing. A two-part entanglement-breaking test distinguishes loss of information from loss of algorithmic efficiency. The hidden subgroup problem illustrates the distinction: among the cases examined, cross-copy coherence is information-theoretically necessary only for the symmetric group. We present this as a diagnostic methodology rather than a theory of quantum advantage: for a new claim, it identifies the relevant adversary, separates the mechanisms a protocol uses from those shown to be necessary, and records the strength of the evidence and the quality of the advantage separately.

item.title: Specifying & Verifying Quantum Error-Correcting Codes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it provides the first machine‑checked framework for specifying and proving properties of quantum error‑correcting codes, turning a historically informal part of the stack into rigorously verified software. By unifying disparate code formalisms in Lean and introducing compositional “code combinators,” the authors can certify distances of large codes—such as confirming IBM’s [[360, 12, 24]] distance—that were previously out of reach for automated analysis. The work paves the way for end‑to‑end verified quantum compilers and architecture‑aware code design, a crucial step toward reliable, scalable quantum hardware.

Building quantum computers is challenging due to the noise that affects qubits. Quantum error correction tackles noise by encoding information in quantum error-correcting (QEC) codes. These codes are often complex, increasingly found by computational search, presented in diverse formalisms with informal arguments, and hard to reason about algorithmically. Given that the rest of the quantum computing stack relies on a QEC code's properties for correct computation, we propose a formally verified foundation for QEC codes. We present QECLean, a Lean-based framework for formally specifying and verifying QEC codes. QECLean backs every claimed QEC-code property with a machine-checked proof, unifies the diverse presentations of codes in the literature through common abstractions, and makes new codes easy to specify. We present a new compositional technique, code combinators, for proving code distance analytically. Code combinators allow us to prove the distance of large codes that are out of reach for algorithmic techniques; for example, we show that IBM's $[[360, 12, \leq 24]]$ code has distance 24, which was previously only known as an upper bound. Furthermore, we show how our approach allows us to formalize and prove entire code families, such as the surface code. Our work lays the foundation required for reasoning about circuit-level implementations of codes on given architectures and for building end-to-end verified compilers for quantum computers. item.title: Stabilizer-Restricted Antidistinguishability in Quantum Computation with Magic States
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that even when quantum computation is limited to adaptive Pauli measurements on magic‑state inputs, the resulting statistics cannot be reproduced by any ontological model that treats independently prepared states as having overlapping hidden‑variable supports, extending the Pusey‑Barrett‑Rudolph argument into the stabilizer‑restricted regime. By linking antidistinguishability to the Clifford hierarchy, it clarifies why classical simulation techniques based on convex‑polytope representations inevitably hit a hard wall for universal QCM, reinforcing magic states as a genuine source of non‑classical power. The result sharpens our theoretical understanding of where quantum advantage originates and warns that any efficient “classical” emulator must abandon preparation independence rather than merely improve sampling heuristics.

An antidistinguishing measurement for a family of preparations excludes at least one preparation for every possible outcome, constraining 'classical' representations of these processes, known as ontological models. We develop this connection within quantum computing with magic states (QCM), a universal model of quantum computation. Our constructions use adaptive Pauli measurements on tensor products of single-qubit non stabilizer states, including families associated with the Clifford hierarchy. These constructions yield stabilizer-restricted versions of the Pusey-Barrett-Rudolph theorem: any ontological model reproducing these measurement statistics and satisfying preparation independence must assign disjoint ontic supports to the preparations considered. We demonstrate this obstruction to preparation independence in a concrete ontological model based on convex polytopes used for the classical simulation of QCM.

item.title: Closing the loop on memory: accurate, shallow and transferable decoding of quantum LDPC codes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the TEMPO‑BP decoder can automatically tune each variable’s memory strength during belief‑propagation, delivering logical failure rates far below those of conventional BP + OSD and Relay‑BP decoders on realistic circuit‑level noise. By achieving comparable or better performance with dramatically fewer iterations and without any code‑specific retuning, the method brings high‑rate qLDPC codes closer to practical fault‑tolerant implementations that promise lower qubit overhead. The results suggest a scalable path for hardware‑friendly decoding, though further testing on larger code families and under varied noise models will be needed before deployment in full quantum processors.

Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes have attracted interest for fault-tolerant quantum computing because their high-rate constructions offer a route to reduced qubit overhead. Realizing this potential requires reliable decoding. Belief propagation (BP) forms the basis of many qLDPC decoders, but can fail to converge under circuit-level noise. Memory-based variants can improve convergence, yet selecting memory strengths that work reliably across different syndromes remains challenging. Here we introduce TEMPO-BP, which adapts each variable's memory strength to the evolving decoding state through local feedback. On the gross code at a physical error rate of 0.4%, single-run TEMPO-BP achieves a per-shot logical failure rate of 0.73%, compared with 2.51% for BP+OSD+CS-10. Ensembles of 10-15 concurrent instances match or lower failure counts relative to Relay-BP-5 at all ten tested operating points, with per-instance iteration caps at least tenfold lower than its serial limit. Without retuning, the gross-code parameters yield fewer observed failures than Relay-BP-5 in its published gross-code configuration across four additional code families. Ablations support state-dependent memory control, while a loop-gain analysis characterizes specific amplification modes in the decoding dynamics.

item.title: Success Probability of Block-Encoding Methods
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article spotlights a hidden cost in many block‑encoding algorithms—namely the probability of successful postselection—and shows how it can dominate the shot budget for realistic Hamiltonians such as the Hubbard model. By deriving concrete bounds for LCU, qubitization and QSVT and demonstrating that favorable Chebyshev degrees or tight polynomial normalizations can dramatically improve success rates, the work gives practitioners a practical knob to tune when designing quantum‑simulation pipelines. Including these probabilities in resource estimates will make future claims about algorithmic speedups far more credible, especially as hardware moves toward the tens‑of‑qubits regime where every shot counts.

Block-encoding methods apply nonunitary functions $f(\widetilde H)$ of a normalized Hermitian operator on a quantum computer, but only upon a successful postselection, which introduces a shot overhead rarely included in resource estimates. We analyze the success probability $p^{(f)}_{\mathrm{success}}=\sum_n w_n|f(\tilde E_n)|^2$ of three constructions, namely linear combination of unitaries (LCU), qubitization and quantum singular value transformation (QSVT), where $w_n$ are the weights of the input state on the eigenstates of $\widetilde H$. Using the one-dimensional Hubbard model with up to 14 sites (35 qubits), we show that for LCU, the success probability is bounded by the squared ratio between the spectral norm and the $1$-norm of the Pauli decomposition, and that for a Hartree--Fock input it plateaus with system size while the ground-state overlap keeps decreasing. For qubitization, it oscillates with the Chebyshev degree, and favorable degrees can be identified from a few dominant spectral components or predicted from shallow-degree data. For QSVT, the polynomial normalization constant directly sets the success probability, and a tight certified bound balances it against phase-finding robustness. An application to quantum Krylov methods shows a nonuniform shot overhead across Krylov moments. The success probability should therefore be part of the resource estimation of block-encoding-based algorithms.

item.title: Variational Corrections to Strong-Disorder Renormalization in the Two-Dimensional Random Transverse Field Ising Model on Quantum Hardware
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how a classic strong‑disorder renormalization‑group (SDRG) flow can be turned into a shallow, hardware‑friendly quantum circuit and then refined with variational optimization, delivering the first experimental demonstration of such an approach for a two‑dimensional random transverse‑field Ising model. By achieving up to 97 % relative energy accuracy on a 49‑qubit superconducting processor, it proves that RG‑derived ansätze can scale beyond the few‑qubit regime and capture correlations missed by the approximate RG itself—an important step toward using near‑term quantum devices for realistic disordered many‑body problems. Strong-disorder renormalization-group (SDRG) methods provide an effective description of disordered quantum many-body systems by identifying the dominant couplings for the low energy physics. However, the resulting renormalization-group flow is approximate and neglects correlations beyond the RG description. Here, we investigate whether variational quantum optimization can be used to correct these approximations. Building on the emergent-coupling-based ansatz (ECBA) developed for the one-dimensional random Heisenberg model, we introduce a formulation adapted to the two-dimensional random transverse field Ising model. The SDRG flow determines the structure of the circuit, while variational optimization allows the state to deviate from the RG approximation. We study the resulting ansatz numerically and experimentally on an IQM superconducting quantum processor. For a 16-qubit system, we perform full variational optimization on the quantum processor, while a 49-qubit system is investigated using pre-optimized parameters, achieving a relative energy accuracy of 89% and 97%, respectively. Our results demonstrate that RG information can be translated into shallow, hardware-compatible quantum circuits while variational optimization enables corrections beyond the underlying RG approximation also for two-dimensional systems.

item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a core obstacle in quantum‑field‑theory simulations by presenting a scalable way to prepare localized wave packets directly from the interacting vacuum, which is essential for realistic scattering experiments on quantum hardware. It extends recent variational and Lorentz‑symmetry techniques to ensure that the prepared states converge correctly in the continuum limit, offering clear diagnostics of Airy‑type distortions and their mitigation as lattice spacing is refined. The work gives practitioners concrete guidance on parameter regimes for reliable two‑particle scattering studies, a step forward as experimental groups target small‑scale φ⁴ simulations on superconducting or trapped‑ion platforms. Nonetheless, the observed artificial inelasticity from coarse digitization highlights that finer field encoding and error mitigation will still be required for quantitatively accurate results.

Probing real-time dynamics is essential for understanding non-perturbative scattering and interactions in quantum field theory. A common challenge in real-time simulation is preparing accurate asymptotic incoming states. Through efficiently solvable eigenvalue problems, we jointly optimize a superposition of single particle momentum eigenstates and a single site interpolating operator to maximize preparation fidelity from the interacting vacuum. This leads to a localized excitation in the interacting theory analogous to a position eigenstate. Weighted sums of the resulting interpolating operator over lattice sites prepare wave packets of arbitrary spatial extent. To ensure that this construction produces the correct continuum limit, relative phases among single particle momentum eigenstates in this superposition are calibrated using a relation derived from Lorentz symmetry. Analyzing single particle wave packet propagation through the position space profile reveals oscillatory Airy distortions, which originate from interference between saddle point contributions at different momenta that share the same lattice group velocity. These oscillations systematically weaken when approaching the continuum limit, and reliable regimes are identified as a function of simulation time and wave packet momentum profile. Two-particle scattering simulations in interacting scalar field theory are also implemented, revealing artificial inelasticity arising from coarse local field digitization or deviation from the Nyquist-Shannon sampling point. With these artifacts under control, present simulations provide emerging evidence for physical inelastic processes in $φ^4$ theory. The constructions introduced in this work may provide new understanding of state preparation for the quantum simulation of scattering.

item.title: Complex fluid flow dynamics by bright scattershot boson sampling
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a photonic boson‑sampling device can be repurposed as a high‑dimensional analog processor for simulating nonlinear fluid dynamics, extending the scattershot approach to “bright” regimes that harvest every generated photon number pattern. By demonstrating accurate forecasts of an eight‑parameter convection model and a 16‑parameter atmospheric circulation model—while tolerating up to 50 % loss—the work positions boson sampling as a competitive alternative to classical reservoir computers for time‑series prediction. The result bridges fundamental quantum optics with practical sensing and modeling tasks, suggesting that near‑term photonic hardware could accelerate complex flow simulations without requiring full fault‑tolerant quantum computers. However, the performance gains are currently demonstrated in simulation, so experimental validation will be key to confirming scalability beyond the digital twin.

Boson sampling machines have become a fruitful tool for establishing new concepts, which connect fundamental physics with computer science applications. Here, we exploit the intrinsically high-dimensional correlations generated by the measurement outcomes of a multiphoton boson sampling machine and demonstrate how a reconfigurable architecture can be programmed to autonomously model the time evolution of nonlinear dynamical systems that describe complex fluid flows. By extending on the original scattershot boson sampling (SBS) scheme to include higher photon number components -- a scheme which we label bright scattershot boson sampling (BSBS) --- this scheme overcomes scaling issues inherent to SBS-based schemes by utilizing all randomly generated input photon number distributions. We illustrate the capability of this scheme for two complex fluid-flow models: an eight-dimensional Lorenz-type model of two-dimensional thermally driven convection and a 16-dimensional model of global atmospheric circulation. Using a digital twin of the BSBS architecture based on multiphoton statistics, we show that the photonic approach accurately reproduces the temporal dynamics of both systems while being resilient to photon losses of up to 50 per cent. We also verified that the BSBS case outperforms a comparable run with coherent light. Moreover, its prediction horizon exceeds that of a classical reservoir-computing model with the same query complexity. These results highlight the potential of near-term photonic quantum computing for addressing relevant real-world tasks on noisy intermediate-scale devices.

item.title: Agentic AI for Discovering Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a large‑language‑model agent can automatically synthesize fault‑tolerant Clifford circuits across a suite of logical‑code tasks, turning what has been a painstaking hand‑crafted process into an evolvable program‑generation pipeline. By coupling the model’s pretrained knowledge with a rigorous circuit verifier, the approach delivers verified, exhaustive fault‑coverage for state preparation, gate design and code‑switching—capabilities that have only recently begun to be explored with machine learning in quantum compilation. If the method scales to larger codes and non‑Clifford operations, it could dramatically shorten the hardware‑software co‑design cycle needed to bring truly error‑corrected quantum processors toward practical advantage.

Scaling quantum computing toward practical quantum advantage is currently limited by the efficiency of circuits that operate on information encoded by quantum error-correcting codes. The full stack of quantum computing encompasses several tasks: preparation of logical code states, implementation of logical gates, logical routines on encoded qubits, etc. Yet, these circuits are largely designed by hand for individual cases, with some recent works incorporating machine learning for certain aspects. We formulate this problem as agentic evolutionary program synthesis, wherein a large language model, leveraging its pretraining knowledge and tool-use proficiency, and guided by a circuit verifier, evolves a program that defines a Clifford circuit for a wide range of curated tasks such as logical state preparation, logical gate design, and logical routines such as code-switching, code growth, etc. Our approach consistently finds fault-tolerant circuits for all of these tasks, each verified by an exhaustive check over faults.

item.title: Solution of the Qubit Marginal Problem from Fermionic Representability
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers the first exact solution of the qubit marginal problem by translating it into fermionic representability, a move that bridges two traditionally separate formalisms and unlocks powerful N‑representability hierarchies for ordinary qubits. By showing that low‑order positivity constraints already capture the ground‑state physics of frustrated Heisenberg and transverse‑field Ising chains to sub‑percent accuracy, it offers a practical, analytically tractable tool for both classical simulation and error mitigation on near‑term quantum hardware. The result positions marginal‑compatibility checks as a new diagnostic layer for quantum processors, though its effectiveness beyond one‑dimensional spin models remains an open question.

Whether local reduced states are compatible with a global quantum state---the quantum marginal problem---is central to quantum information and simulation. Here we present a solution to the ensemble marginal problem for qubits based on the representability theory of fermions. Encoding each qubit as one fermion in two orbitals, we prove that the representable qubit marginals form an exposed face of the set of $N$-representable fermionic reduced density matrices, selected by the vanishing of every site-occupation variance. Complete hierarchies of fermionic representability conditions therefore transfer exactly to qubits. Applications to frustrated Heisenberg and transverse-field Ising rings show that the $(2,3)$-positivity conditions are exact at the Majumdar--Ghosh point and accurate to about 0.5% at criticality. Because the conditions hold for any quantum state, they also provide a framework for mitigating measurement errors on qubit-based quantum devices.

item.title: Dissipation as a Resource for Entanglement via High-Spin Mediator Purification
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that engineered dissipation can actively purify a thermally mixed high‑spin impurity and turn it into a powerful entangling bus, achieving a negativity of 0.64 at 12 K—far above the temperatures where most solid‑state spin qubits retain coherence. By demonstrating a non‑monotonic optimum pump rate, the work links recent advances in optical pumping of magnetic atoms to practical hardware designs that exploit rather than suppress decoherence channels. The result suggests a new route to robust two‑qubit gates in impurity‑based platforms, though scaling will require careful management of the same dissipative coupling that delivers the entanglement.

We study entanglement generation between two spin qubits mediated by a single, thermally mixed, high-spin ($S=5/2$) magnetic impurity, using the Lindblad master equation to compare coherent and dissipative control of the mediator. We show that no coherent drive, however strong or resonant, can purify the mediator beyond its thermal value --- a direct consequence of unitary evolution exactly preserving state purity --- while a dissipative channel purifies it up to the limit set by the optical pumping cycle itself, $\mathrm{Tr}[ρ_M^2]\approx0.8$. Modeling this channel with rates fixed by the measured optical pumping of a single Mn spin, we find that the entanglement it enables is not monotonic in the pump strength: it peaks at a finite rate and then decreases, since the same channel leaks decoherence to the qubits through the coupling that mediates their entanglement. At the experimental pumping rate, a single $80$ns pulse purifies the mediator, the resulting polarization persists for a timescale three orders of magnitude longer than the entangling dynamics, and the first-recurrence negativity rises from $0.18$ to $0.64$ at $12$K, remaining above $0.6$ up to $30$K. These results establish dissipation, not as noise to be suppressed, but as the very resource that makes robust entanglement generation possible.

item.title: Tessa: Encoding Classical Data Across an Entire Quantum Processor
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it tackles the long‑standing data‑loading bottleneck by showing how to map thousands of classical values directly onto a quantum processor without any SWAP routing, leveraging the native coupling graph of the hardware. By extending earlier QPIXL and QCrank ideas into a checkerboard layout that pairs address and data qubits, Tessa demonstrates scalable state preparation on IBM’s Phoenix and Fez devices—an advance that could accelerate near‑term quantum‑machine‑learning and quantum‑simulation workflows. The approach is still constrained by readout noise and the degree of local connectivity, but it proves that device‑aware encoding can be realized today on real hardware.

We present Tessa, a hardware-aware, device-wide scheme to encode classical data on quantum computers. We use it to experimentally encode and decode up to $1568$ real values using IBM's Phoenix and Fez quantum computers on a variety of data. Tessa's construction is an extension of QPIXL and QCrank. However, it checkerboards address and data qubits across a coupling graph with neighbouring data qubits sharing only a subset of address qubits. When using the device's coupling graph no SWAP gates or routing is required, but the construction works for any bipartite coupling graph. The shots required for readout are determined by the local coupling degree. As examples, we have used cat states (pixel art of cats), various pixel art, audio, MIDI, DNA sequences and protein amino acid sequences.
